title: Reading without niqqud
topic: guessing the vowels from context and word patterns
why: On to real reading without vowels, with three strategies: recognizing frequent words, spotting the prefixes ו ה ב ל מ ש, and guessing verbs from the present-tense pattern (כּוֹתֵב / כּוֹתֶבֶת). Sentences are given with and without niqqud, so you can read a menu or a sign the way people do in Israel.

Words you recognize at a glance

An Israeli reader doesn't decode letter by letter: they recognize frequent words like pictures, exactly as you do with \"the\" or \"and\" in English. Learn them first without vowels:

Without vowelsWith vowelsMeaning
אניאֲנִיI, me [ani]
הוא / היאהוּא / הִיאhe / she [hu / hi]
זה / זאתזֶה / זֹאתthis (is), it's (m. / f.) [ze / zot]
מה / מימָה / מִיwhat? / who? [ma / mi]
כן / לאכֵּן / לֹאyes / no [ken / lo]
ישיֵשׁthere is [yesh]
טוב / מאודטוֹב / מְאוֹדgood / very [tov / me'od]

Without the dots, ש can be shin or sin: יש is read yesh, but ישראל is read yisra'el. Once again, it's the word you know that decides.

", "

Little attached words: ו ה ב ל מ ש

In Hebrew, \"and\", \"the\", \"in\", \"to\", \"from\" and \"that\" are not separate words: a single letter attaches to the front of the word. Without vowels, spot this prefix first, then read the word that's left.

PrefixMeaningWith vowelsWithout vowelsSound
וandסָבָא וְסַבְתָּאסבא וסבתאsaba ve-savta
הtheהַבַּיִתהביתha-bayit
בin, atבַּבַּיִתבביתba-bayit
לto, towardלַיָּםליםla-yam
מfromמֵהַבַּיִתמהביתme-ha-bayit
שthat, whoyou'll see it latershe

With ב and ל, the ה of \"the\" disappears: you write בבית (ba-bayit, in the house), never בהבית.

The trap: not every first letter is a prefix! In שלום, בית, לילה or מאוד, it's part of the word. If, once you remove the letter, what's left isn't a word you know, it's not a prefix.

", "

Patterns: a mold for the present tense

Many verbs in the present tense follow the same mold: a ו after the first letter, read o, then an e. In the feminine, you add a ת at the end: -et. In English, the present changes a little with the person (I write, she writes); in Hebrew, it doesn't change with the person at all, but with gender: אֲנִי לוֹמֵד (a man), אֲנִי לוֹמֶדֶת (a woman).

With vowelsWithout vowelsSoundMeaning
כּוֹתֵב / כּוֹתֶבֶתכותב / כותבתkotev / kotevetwrite(s)
לוֹמֵד / לוֹמֶדֶתלומד / לומדתlomed / lomedetlearn(s)
עוֹבֵד / עוֹבֶדֶתעובד / עובדתoved / ovedetwork(s)
אוֹכֵל / אוֹכֶלֶתאוכל / אוכלתokhel / okheleteat(s)

When you see a four-letter word with ו in second position, try o-e: הולך = holekh (he goes); with ת at the end: הולכת = holekhet (she goes). Two variants: קוֹרֵא / קוֹרֵאת (kore / koret, read(s)), where the א is silent, and שׁוֹתֶה / שׁוֹתָה (shote / shota, drink(s)), with the final ה from the previous lesson: e in the masculine, a in the feminine.

נועה לומדת עברית.The same sentence, without vowels.
